claim: Hypoxia and consequent production of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) promote blood vessel leakiness and edema in ocular diseases.
source: Hypoxia and consequent production of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) promote blood vessel leakiness and edema in ocular diseases.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field of ocular disease pathology.

claim: Anti-VEGFA therapeutics may aggravate hypoxia.
source: Anti-VEGFA therapeutics may aggravate hypoxia
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known concern with anti-VEGFA therapy.

claim: Suppression of NO formation resulted in reduced retinal neoangiogenesis.
source: Suppression of NO formation resulted in reduced retinal neoangiogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Remaining vascular tufts exhibited reduced vascular leakage through stabilized endothelial adherens junctions when NO formation was suppressed.
source: Remaining vascular tufts exhibited reduced vascular leakage through stabilized endothelial adherens junctions, manifested as reduced phosphorylation of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin Y685 in a c-Src-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing reduced VE-cadherin Y685 phosphorylation.

claim: Reduced vascular leakage with NO suppression is manifested as reduced phosphorylation of VE-cadherin Y685 in a c-Src-dependent manner.
source: Remaining vascular tufts exhibited reduced vascular leakage through stabilized endothelial adherens junctions, manifested as reduced phosphorylation of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin Y685 in a c-Src-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including PLA assays and immunostaining.

claim: Treatment with a single dose of L-NMMA in established retinopathy restored the vascular barrier and prevented leakage.
source: Treatment with a single dose of L-NMMA in established retinopathy restored the vascular barrier and prevented leakage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by microsphere leakage assay data in Figure 5.

claim: NO destabilizes adherens junctions, resulting in vascular hyperpermeability, by converging with the VEGFA/VEGFR2/c-Src/VE-cadherin pathway.
source: We conclude that NO destabilizes adheren junctions, resulting in vascular hyperpermeability, by converging with the VEGFA/VEGFR2/c-Src/VE-cadherin pathway.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pathological neovascularization is intimately associated with the progression of several retinal diseases, including retinopathy of prematurity, diabetic retinopathy, and exudative age-related macular degeneration.
source: Pathological neovascularization is intimately associated with the progression of several retinal diseases, including retinopathy of prematurity, diabetic retinopathy, and exudative age-related macular degeneration.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, presented in the introduction.

claim: Neovascularization occurs in response to hypoxia, tissue ischemia, and the consequent production of angiogenic agonists, such as VEGFA.
source: Neovascularization occurs in response to hypoxia, tissue ischemia, and the consequent production of angiogenic agonists, such as vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA), a potent inducer of vessel formation and vascular leakage (Campochiaro, 2015; Semenza, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VEGFA is a potent inducer of vessel formation and vascular leakage.
source: Neovascularization occurs in response to hypoxia, tissue ischemia, and the consequent production of angiogenic agonists, such as vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA), a potent inducer of vessel formation and vascular leakage (Campochiaro, 2015; Semenza, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: New vessels formed during retinal ischemia are often dysfunctional and fail to stabilize.
source: The new vessels formed during retinal ischemia are often dysfunctional and fail to stabilize (Fruttiger, 2007; Krock et al., 2011), leading to vessel leakage or hemorrhaging and to retinal detachment, visual impairment, and even blindness.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysfunctional vessels in retinal ischemia lead to vessel leakage or hemorrhaging and to retinal detachment, visual impairment, and even blindness.
source: The new vessels formed during retinal ischemia are often dysfunctional and fail to stabilize (Fruttiger, 2007; Krock et al., 2011), leading to vessel leakage or hemorrhaging and to retinal detachment, visual impairment, and even blindness.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Suppression of neoangiogenesis and retinal edema is a therapeutic goal in the treatment of ischemic eye diseases.
source: Therefore, suppression of neoangiogenesis, and thereby, retinal edema, is a therapeutic goal in the treatment of ischemic eye diseases (Daruich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept decrease neovascular formation as well as edema.
source: A number of therapeutic options designed to neutralize VEGFA by preventing binding to its receptor, VEGF receptor 2 (VEGFR2), such as bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept, decrease neovascular formation as well as edema (Mintz-Hittner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Anti-VEGF therapies do not correct the underlying hypoxia and vessel regression may instead further aggravate hypoxia.
source: However, they do not correct the underlying hypoxia; in fact, vessel regression may instead further aggravate hypoxia.
evidence: This is a statement of known limitations of anti-VEGF therapy.

claim: Anti-VEGF therapies can induce an elevation in intraocular pressure and hemorrhaging in many cases.
source: Moreover, in many cases, anti-VEGF therapies can induce an elevation in intraocular pressure and hemorrhaging (Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Repeated intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF-therapy present a potential for infections and scarring.
source: The repeated intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF-therapy present a potential for infections and scarring (Patel et al., 2013)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Side effects of anti-VEGF therapy including disrupted neural development in infants have been reported.
source: in addition, side effects including disrupted neural development in infants have been reported (Canadian Neonatal Network and the Canadian Neonatal Follow-Up Network Investigators et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is a clear need for developing new treatments to suppress proangiogenic stimuli while also achieving a long-lasting effect with safe administration.
source: Thus, even though the current therapy improves vision for many patients in the early phases of disease, there is a clear need for developing new treatments to suppress proangiogenic stimuli while also achieving a long-lasting effect with safe administration.
evidence: This is a statement of the rationale for the study based on limitations of current therapies.

claim: Angiogenesis and vascular permeability in the retina are initiated by the VEGFA/VEGFR2 signaling pathway.
source: Angiogenesis and vascular permeability in the retina are initiated by the VEGFA/VEGFR2 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: VEGFR2 is found not only on blood vascular endothelial cells but also on neuronal cells in the retina.
source: VEGFR2 is found not only on blood vascular endothelial cells but also on neuronal cells in the retina, likely contributing to the side effect of VEGFA/VEGFR2 suppression on neural development in premature infants (Nishijima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VEGFR2 expression on neuronal cells likely contributes to the side effect of VEGFA/VEGFR2 suppression on neural development in premature infants.
source: VEGFR2 is found not only on blood vascular endothelial cells but also on neuronal cells in the retina, likely contributing to the side effect of VEGFA/VEGFR2 suppression on neural development in premature infants (Nishijima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of Y1212 in VEGFR2 is required for activation of phosphatidyl inositol three kinase and AKT.
source: Phosphorylation of Y1212 in VEGFR2 is required for activation of phosphatidyl inositol three kinase and AKT (Testini et al., 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of Y949 in VEGFR2 is required for activation of the c-Src pathway and regulation of vascular permeability through VE-cadherin.
source: while phosphorylation of Y949 is required for activation of the c-Src pathway and regulation of vascular permeability through vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions.
source: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions, strongly implicated in regulation of vascular permeability, leakage, and associated edema (Giannotta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VE-cadherin is strongly implicated in regulation of vascular permeability, leakage, and associated edema.
source: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions, strongly implicated in regulation of vascular permeability, leakage, and associated edema (Giannotta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Y685 residue in VE-cadherin correlates with VEGFA-induced vascular hyperpermeability.
source: In particular, phosphorylation of the Y685 residue in VE-cadherin correlates with VEGFA-induced vascular hyperpermeability (Smith et al., 2020; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: eNOS is activated downstream of VEGFA through phosphorylation on S1177 (S1176 in mice) by AKT.
source: Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), activated downstream of VEGFA through phosphorylation on S1177 (S1176 in mice) by AKT (Fulton et al., 1999), produces nitric oxide (NO) and regulates vascular permeability.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: eNOS produces nitric oxide (NO) and regulates vascular permeability.
source: Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), activated downstream of VEGFA through phosphorylation on S1177 (S1176 in mice) by AKT (Fulton et al., 1999), produces nitric oxide (NO) and regulates vascular permeability.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mice with a constitutive eNOS gene (Nos3) inactivation show reduced extravasation of bovine serum albumin in the healthy skin in response to VEGFA challenge.
source: Both mice with a constitutive eNOS gene (Nos3) inactivation (Fukumura et al., 2001) and mice expressing an eNOS serine to alanine point mutation (S1176A) (Nos3S1176A/S1176A) (Di Lorenzo et al., 2013) show reduced extravasation of bovine serum albumin in the healthy skin in response to VEGFA challenge.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mice expressing an eNOS serine to alanine point mutation (S1176A) show reduced extravasation of bovine serum albumin in the healthy skin in response to VEGFA challenge.
source: Both mice with a constitutive eNOS gene (Nos3) inactivation (Fukumura et al., 2001) and mice expressing an eNOS serine to alanine point mutation (S1176A) (Nos3S1176A/S1176A) (Di Lorenzo et al., 2013) show reduced extravasation of bovine serum albumin in the healthy skin in response to VEGFA challenge.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An important mediator of the effect of eNOS-generated NO is the relaxation of peri-vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs), leading to increased vessel diameter and enhanced blood flow and thereby flow-driven vascular sieving.
source: An important mediator of the effect of eNOS-generated NO is the relaxation of peri-vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs), leading to increased vessel diameter and enhanced blood flow and thereby flow-driven vascular sieving (Sessa, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: eNOS activity correlates with tyrosine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin in cultured endothelial cells.
source: In addition, eNOS activity correlates with tyrosine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin in cultured endothelial cells (Di Lorenzo et al., 2013), providing a mechanism for how eNOS activity may directly affect vascular permeability, distinct from vasodilation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: eNOS activity may directly affect vascular permeability through a mechanism distinct from vasodilation.
source: In addition, eNOS activity correlates with tyrosine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin in cultured endothelial cells (Di Lorenzo et al., 2013), providing a mechanism for how eNOS activity may directly affect vascular permeability, distinct from vasodilation.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The healthy retinal vasculature is protected by a stringent blood-retinal barrier.
source: In contrast to the skin vasculature, the healthy retinal vasculature is protected by a stringent blood-retinal barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In retinal diseases, the blood-retinal barrier is disrupted, leading to increased vascular permeability.
source: In retinal diseases, the barrier is disrupted, leading to increased vascular permeability (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: NO and related reactive oxygen species (ROS) are important pathogenic agents in retinopathy.
source: In accordance, NO and related reactive oxygen species (ROS) are important pathogenic agents in retinopathy (Opatrilova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Suppressed NO formation via the use of L-NMMA negates neovascular tuft formation and vascular leakage during retinal disease.
source: Here, we show that suppressed NO formation via the use of the competitive NOS inhibitor, Nω-Methyl-l-arginine (L-NMMA), which inhibits NO formation from all three NOS variants (eNOS, inducible NOS, and neuronal NOS), or an eNOS mutant, S1176A, negates neovascular tuft formation and vascular leakage during retinal disease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: An eNOS mutant, S1176A, negates neovascular tuft formation and vascular leakage during retinal disease.
source: Here, we show that suppressed NO formation via the use of the competitive NOS inhibitor, Nω-Methyl-l-arginine (L-NMMA), which inhibits NO formation from all three NOS variants (eNOS, inducible NOS, and neuronal NOS), or an eNOS mutant, S1176A, negates neovascular tuft formation and vascular leakage during retinal disease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: NO promotes c-Src Y418 phosphorylation at endothelial junctions.
source: Mechanistically, NO promotes c-Src Y418 phosphorylation at endothelial junctions and phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at Y685, required for dismantling of adherens junctions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding of the study supported by PLA and immunostaining data.

claim: NO promotes phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at Y685, required for dismantling of adherens junctions.
source: Mechanistically, NO promotes c-Src Y418 phosphorylation at endothelial junctions and phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at Y685, required for dismantling of adherens junctions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of NO formation by L-NMMA treatment suppresses vascular leakage from established neovascular tufts.
source: Inhibition of NO formation by L-NMMA treatment suppresses vascular leakage also from established neovascular tufts, separating regulation of leakage from the angiogenic process as such.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by microsphere leakage data.

claim: L-NMMA treatment separates regulation of leakage from the angiogenic process.
source: Inhibition of NO formation by L-NMMA treatment suppresses vascular leakage also from established neovascular tufts, separating regulation of leakage from the angiogenic process as such.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Mice expressing a VE-cadherin tyrosine to phenylalanine mutation (VEC-Y685F) are resistant to eNOS inhibition.
source: Mice expressing a VE-cadherin tyrosine to phenylalanine mutation (VEC-Y685F) are resistant to eNOS inhibition, supporting the model that NO regulates adherens junctions through direct effects on c-Src and VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: NO regulates adherens junctions through direct effects on c-Src and VE-cadherin.
source: Mice expressing a VE-cadherin tyrosine to phenylalanine mutation (VEC-Y685F) are resistant to eNOS inhibition, supporting the model that NO regulates adherens junctions through direct effects on c-Src and VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by experimental data.

claim: eNOS/NO promote vascular permeability through the established effect on vSMC relaxation and increased flow-driven permeability to solute and small molecules in the precapillary arterial bed.
source: These data suggest that eNOS/NO promote vascular permeability not only through the established effect on vSMC relaxation and increased flow-driven permeability to solute and small molecules in the precapillary arterial bed, but also through disruption of adherens junctions allowing leakage of larger molecules from the postcapillary venular bed.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: eNOS/NO promote vascular permeability through disruption of adherens junctions allowing leakage of larger molecules from the postcapillary venular bed.
source: These data suggest that eNOS/NO promote vascular permeability not only through the established effect on vSMC relaxation and increased flow-driven permeability to solute and small molecules in the precapillary arterial bed, but also through disruption of adherens junctions allowing leakage of larger molecules from the postcapillary venular bed.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Nitric oxide formation is significantly higher in Nos3+/+ mice compared to Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice as measured by Griess assay.
source: Figure 1C
evidence: Figure 1C shows quantification of NO formation using a Griess assay, with Nos3+/+ showing approximately 8 µM NO2- + NO3- compared to approximately 1 µM in Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice (p<0.0001).

claim: Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice show reduced pathological tuft area compared to Nos3+/+ mice after OIR-challenge at P17.
source: After OIR-challenge, Nos3S1176A/S1176A P17 retinas showed reduced pathological tuft area compared to Nos3+/+ (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification in Figure 1E showing approximately 10% tuft area in Nos3+/+ versus approximately 6% in Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice.

claim: The extent of avascularity was the same between Nos3S1176A/S1176A and Nos3+/+ mice after OIR-challenge.
source: while the extent of avascularity was the same (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification in Figure 1F showing approximately 17% avascular area in both genotypes.

claim: The average size of individual tufts was reduced in the Nos3S1176A/S1176A pups compared to Nos3+/+ after OIR.
source: The average size of individual tufts was reduced in the Nos3S1176A/S1176A pups (Figure 1G)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification in Figure 1G showing median tuft size of approximately 16,000 µm² in Nos3+/+ versus approximately 10,000 µm² in Nos3S1176A/S1176A.

claim: The total number of tufts formed after OIR was unaffected between Nos3S1176A/S1176A and Nos3+/+ mice.
source: while the total number of tufts formed after OIR was unaffected (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification in Figure 1H showing approximately 100 tufts per retina in both genotypes.

claim: Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice showed normal postnatal vascular development.
source: The suppressed formation of neoangiogenic tufts in the absence of eNOS S1176 phosphorylation was not due to developmental defects as Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice showed normal postnatal vascular development.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing no differences in vascular area, outgrowth, filopodia length, tip cell number, or branch points at P7.

claim: At P12 after OIR-challenge, there was no difference in the degree of avascularity in the retina between Nos3S1176A/S1176A and Nos3+/+ pups.
source: At P12 after OIR-challenge, there was also no difference in the degree of avascularity in the retina between Nos3S1176A/S1176A and Nos3+/+ pups, indicating that the strains responded similarly to the hyperoxic challenge (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No differences were found when comparing Nos3+/+ and Nos3S1176A/S1176A retinas with regard to coverage of vessels by NG2-positive pericytes at P17.
source: Moreover, no differences were found when comparing Nos3+/+ and Nos3S1176A/S1176A retinas with regard to coverage of vessels by NG2-positive pericytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: No differences were found when comparing Nos3+/+ and Nos3S1176A/S1176A retinas with regard to the presence of CD68-positive macrophages at P17.
source: Moreover, no differences were found when comparing Nos3+/+ and Nos3S1176A/S1176A retinas with regard to coverage of vessels by NG2-positive pericytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B) or the presence of CD68-positive macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), at P17.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Vessel perfusion was enhanced in Nos3S1176A/S1176A tufts compared to the wild type.
source: However, vessel perfusion was enhanced in Nos3S1176A/S1176A tufts compared to the wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F), most likely due to the smaller tufts formed in the Nos3S1176A/S1176A retinas.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: The reduced tuft area in the Nos3S1176A/S1176A condition was not a result of differences in Nos3 or Nos2 expression between the Nos3+/+ and Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice before or after the OIR-challenge.
source: Importantly, the reduced tuft area in the Nos3S1176A/S1176A condition was not a result of differences in Nos3 or Nos2 expression between the Nos3+/+ and Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice before or after the OIR-challenge (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: Reduced tuft area was not a result of reduced VEGFA production as an equally induced level of VEGFA was seen in the mutant and wild-type retinas.
source: Reduced tuft area was also not a result of reduced VEGFA production as an equally induced level of VEGFA was seen in the mutant and wild-type retinas (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The low relative expression level of Nos2 compared to Nos3 emphasizes the primary role of eNOS as a source of endothelial NO, both in the unchallenged and OIR-treated condition.
source: It should also be noted that the low relative expression level of Nos2 (encoding inducible nitric oxide synthase [iNOS]) compared to Nos3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D,E) emphasizes the primary role of eNOS as a source of endothelial NO, both in the unchallenged and OIR-treated condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text and supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D,E.

claim: VEGFA produced during the relative hypoxia phase (P12–P17) is an important instigator of edema in retinopathy.
source: VEGFA produced during the relative hypoxia phase (P12–P17) is an important instigator of edema in retinopathy (Connor et al., 2009; Dor et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VEGFA/VEGFR2 signaling and vessel leakage correlates with phosphorylation of VE-cadherin on Y685.
source: VEGFA/VEGFR2 signaling and vessel leakage correlates with phosphorylation of VE-cadherin on Y685 (Li et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2020; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: pY685 VE-cadherin immunostaining, normalized to the total VE-cadherin area, was significantly lower in Nos3S1176A/S1176A tufts than in the WT tufts.
source: pY685 VE-cadherin immunostaining, normalized to the total VE-cadherin area, was significantly lower in Nos3S1176A/S1176A tufts than in the WT tufts (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2A,B.

claim: eNOS was phosphorylated on S1177 in VEGFA-treated human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMEC).
source: eNOS was phosphorylated on S1177 in VEGFA-treated human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMEC).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Induction of eNOS phosphorylation appeared with similar kinetics but slightly more potently by VEGFA than by histamine.
source: Induction of eNOS phosphorylation appeared with similar kinetics but slightly more potently by VEGFA than by the inflammatory mediator histamine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Histamine is a well-known inducer of eNOS activity.
source: Induction of eNOS phosphorylation appeared with similar kinetics but slightly more potently by VEGFA than by the inflammatory mediator histamine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D for antibody validation), a well-known inducer of eNOS activity (Thors et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: eNOS phosphorylation was accompanied by NO production in response to VEGFA stimulation, as assessed using the fluorescent probe, DAF-FM DA.
source: eNOS phosphorylation was accompanied by NO production in response to VEGFA stimulation, as assessed using the fluorescent probe, DAF-FM DA added to the HRMEC culture medium.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by DAF-FM DA assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: NO accumulated significantly by 1 min VEGFA stimulation and still persisted at 10 min.
source: NO accumulated significantly by 1 min stimulation and still persisted at 10 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by DAF-FM DA assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DAF-FM DA fluorescence, and therefore NO production, was blocked by incubating cells with L-NMMA to the level of the untreated control.
source: DAF-FM DA fluorescence, and therefore NO production, was blocked by incubating cells with L-NMMA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), to the level of the untreated control.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by DAF-FM DA assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: VEGFA is a potent inducer of eNOS activity and NO production.
source: Combined, these data show that VEGFA is a potent inducer of eNOS activity and NO production.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin on Y685 correlates with activation of the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase c-Src.
source: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin on Y685 correlates with activation of the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase c-Src (Orsenigo et al., 2012; Wallez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NO-generating reagent, SNAP, can increase the levels of activated c-Src phosphorylated on Y418 in fibroblast cultures.
source: The NO-generating reagent, SNAP, can increase the levels of activated c-Src phosphorylated on Y418 in fibroblast cultures (Rahman et al., 2010), indicating a potential role for NO in c-Src activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: L-NMMA had no effect on VEGFA-induced phosphorylation of eNOS (S1177) in vitro.
source: In vitro, the cell-permeable NOS inhibitor L-NMMA had no effect on VEGFA-induced phosphorylation of eNOS (S1177).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: There was no significant effect of L-NMMA treatment on VEGFA-induced phosphorylation of AKT (S473).
source: There was also no significant effect of L-NMMA treatment on VEGFA-induced phosphorylation of AKT (S473) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: VEGFA-mediated AKT activation is a prerequisite for phosphorylation of eNOS at S1177.
source: VEGFA-mediated AKT activation is a prerequisite for phosphorylation of eNOS at S1177 (Chen and Meyrick, 2004; Schleicher et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at Y685 was attenuated and delayed by L-NMMA treatment.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at Y685 was attenuated and delayed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), an indication of reduced permeability (Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Immunoblotting for SFK Y418 phosphorylation showed a biphasic induction in the control.
source: Immunoblotting for SFK Y418 phosphorylation, representing c-Src activation, showed a biphasic induction in the control.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Treatment with L-NMMA efficiently suppressed the second pY418 peak at 10 min of VEGFA stimulation.
source: Treatment with L-NMMA efficiently suppressed the second pY418 peak at 10 min of VEGFA stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: A leakage-resistant VEGFR2 Y949F mutant lacked the second pY418 peak in immunoblots.
source: The inhibition by L-NMMA of the second Y418 peak observed here mirrors results obtained by Li et al., where a leakage-resistant VEGFR2 Y949F mutant also lacked the second pY418 peak in immunoblots (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Immunostaining for c-Src pY418 failed to reveal differences in pY418 c-Src levels between Nos3+/+ and Nos3 S1176A/S1176A retinas.
source: Upon in vivo analyses, immunostaining for c-Src pY418 however failed to reveal differences in pY418 c-Src levels between Nos3+/+ and Nos3 S1176A/S1176A retinas (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The pY418 antibody is not specific to c-Src phosphorylation and likely recognizes several related Src family kinases (SFKs) such as Yes and Fyn.
source: These results indicate that the pY418 antibody is not specific to c-Src phosphorylation and likely recognizes several related Src family kinases (SFKs) such as Yes and Fyn.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the experimental results.

claim: The double pY418 peaks appearing in the immunoblots may be due to phosphorylation of distinct SFKs.
source: Thus, the double pY418 peaks appearing in the immunoblots may be due to phosphorylation of distinct SFKs.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the text based on the experimental results.

claim: VEGFA stimulation increased PLA spots representing pY418 specifically on c-Src at least fivefold in the isolated endothelial cells (iECs) from Nos+/+ mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, VEGFA stimulation increased PLA spots, representing pY418 specifically on c-Src, at least fivefold in the isolated endothelial cells (iECs) from Nos+/+ mice
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PLA data in Figure 2D.

claim: VEGFA stimulation did not increase PLA spots representing pY418 on c-Src in iECs from Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, VEGFA stimulation increased PLA spots, representing pY418 specifically on c-Src, at least fivefold in the isolated endothelial cells (iECs) from Nos+/+ mice, but not in iECs from Nos3S1176A/S1176A mice
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PLA data in Figure 2D.

claim: The c-Src pY418 PLA spots co-localized with VE-cadherin immunostaining.
source: The c-Src pY418 PLA spots co-localized with VE-cadherin immunostaining (Figure 2E).
